content: 1. Literature reviews emphasize the importance of sustainable funding mechanisms to support community-based health services. 2. Decentralized tuberculosis (TB) services can serve as an effective entry point for integrating care for comorbid conditions. 3. Decentralizing specialist services facilitates the delivery of integrated healthcare, particularly at the community level. 4. The availability and dissemination of guidance and normative documents are essential to promote collaborative healthcare actions. 5. Expanding social protection initiatives is critical to ensuring equitable access to healthcare services. 6. Co-locating screening and treatment services for TB and its comorbidities improves accessibility and care coordination. 7. Mobile clinics that provide care near or at the patient’s home enhance healthcare delivery and accessibility. 8. Training community health workers to screen for both TB and comorbidities is a vital strategy for early detection and intervention. 9. Leveraging the expertise and contact networks of community health workers can significantly expand healthcare access. 10. Community health workers delivering medications directly to patients in their communities improve treatment adherence and outcomes. 11. Psychosocial and family support services are essential components of comprehensive healthcare for TB and comorbidities. 12. Motivating patients to understand their health status encourages proactive health-seeking behaviors. 13. Counseling and educating patients about TB and its comorbidities improve awareness and adherence to treatment regimens. 14. Community education initiatives are necessary to enhance health-seeking behaviors for TB and related conditions. 15. Early disclosure of diabetes comorbidity to TB providers facilitates timely and effective management. 16. Early screening for diabetes in TB patients is crucial for identifying and addressing comorbid conditions. 17. Prompt referral for diabetes management improves glycemic control during TB treatment. 18. Co-management of TB and diabetes by the same primary care physician ensures integrated and effective care. 19. High pill burden and treatment side effects are significant challenges for patients with TB and HIV co-infection. 20. Insufficient funding for transportation prevents patients from attending daily TB treatment support appointments. 21. Fear of stigma and discrimination related to both TB and HIV discourages patients from seeking care. 22. Inadequate food intake to counteract the side effects of combined TB and HIV treatment regimens leads to poor adherence. 23. Knowledge of TB’s curability is essential to encourage patients to complete their treatment. 24. Understanding the severity of TB in the context of HIV co-infection is critical for both patients and healthcare providers. 25. Support from family members and healthcare workers plays a pivotal role in improving treatment adherence and outcomes. 26. Interviews did not delve deeply into the specific needs and expectations for HIV care, as these have been extensively studied in prior research. 27. Findings on HIV care were summarized from previous studies by Daftary et al. (2012) and Gebremariam et al. (2010). 28. Stakeholder consultations and external reviews for the WHO Framework on Collaborative Action for TB and Comorbidities included declarations of interest from all consulted experts. 29. All declarations of interest were evaluated by the WHO secretariat for potential conflicts of interest and presented at the beginning of the stakeholder consultation. 30. Experts such as Aneeta Pasha, Harry Hausler, Jeremy Ross, Mary Rosary Santiago, Phangisile Mtshali, and Zahedul Islam disclosed their affiliations and roles, none of which were deemed conflicts of interest in relation to the framework’s development.
